summary.summary: Oxfordshire took no new borrowing in 2025/26 and let £7m of debt go (a £2m PWLB maturity plus a £5m LOBO its lender called in November 2025), leaving £264.8m of borrowing against a £512.5m capital financing requirement — 48% internally funded — alongside £424m of investments. Treasury income beat budget by £8.2m on higher rates and balances, and the council parked the gains in reserves, including £8.0m added to a High Needs DSG risk reserve in June 2026. The shadow is the schools grant: the negative High Needs DSG balance reached £149.3m by year end, costing an estimated £6.0m in unearned interest this year (£16.4m cumulative since 2019/20) and steadily eating the cash the council can invest.

signals.headline: Negative High Needs DSG balance reached £149.3m by 31 March 2026; estimated £6.0m of unearned interest cost in 2025/26 (up from £3.8m in 2024/25), £16.4m cumulative since 2019/20
signals.why: The deficit behind the statutory override is consuming investable cash at an accelerating rate, and the council is pre-emptively parking £8m of treasury gains in a High Needs risk reserve against it.

signals.headline: A £5m LOBO at 3.68% was called and repaid without penalty on 24 November 2025; four LOBO loans totalling £20m remain
signals.why: Lenders have started exercising their options in this rate environment; the remaining £20m is modest against £424m of investments, so a further call is manageable.

signals.headline: No new external borrowing in 2025/26; debt down from £271.9m to £264.8m against a £512.5m CFR, with internal balances funding 48% of the requirement
signals.why: Shrinking external debt plus £424m of investments leaves little refinancing exposure — only 12.16% of borrowing matures within 12 months against a 20% limit.

news_drafts.headline: Oxfordshire's audit recovery stalls into third year after disclaimed opinion
news_drafts.lead: Oxfordshire County Council remains locked in multi-year audit recovery, with its accounts still unable to receive an unqualified sign-off three years after a complete audit failure. The auditors issued a disclaimer of opinion in 2023/24—the most serious form of audit failure—and a qualified opinion last year. Even by 2025/26, certain valuations and reserve movements will still lack assurance. The auditors have now flagged the council's General Fund Balance, a key measure of financial resilience, as presenting higher inherent risk due to material unaudited movements and susceptibility to management bias. They require confirmation that management can simultaneously rebuild historic records from 2022/23 onwards while delivering current-year audit work, and have signalled they will seek additional audit fees to reflect the scope of extra work required. Recovery remains on track for an unqualified opinion by 2026/27, but the pattern suggests underlying capacity constraints.

findings.paper_title: A&G20260916R7 Internal Audit Progress Report Sept 2026 AG FINAL
findings.headline: Principal Auditor resignation in October 2026; impact on audit plan delivery under review.
findings.detail: One of the Principal Auditors has resigned and is leaving the team in October 2026. The report states that "the resourcing position and impact on delivery of the plan is currently being reviewed." The timing coincides with active delivery of the 2026/27 internal audit plan across multiple ongoing assignments.
findings.matters: Loss of internal audit capacity could impair the council's ability to identify control weaknesses and track remediation of existing findings. Uncertainty about backfill indicates the impact on audit coverage has not yet been determined.
findings.figures: One Principal Auditor leaving October 2026; 2026/27 audit plan includes 21 audits across various stages (fieldwork, scoping, not started)
findings.quote: one of the Principal Auditors has resigned and will be leaving the team in October, the resourcing position and impact on delivery of the plan is currently being reviewed.

findings.paper_title: A&G20260916R7 Internal Audit Progress Report Sept 2026 AG FINAL
findings.headline: School repairs and maintenance budgets not being applied to planned maintenance priorities; council funding emergency reactive works from central capital.
findings.detail: Repairs & Maintenance in Schools audit (rated Amber) found variable practice in schools' use of delegated maintenance budgets with limited corporate oversight. The audit identified examples of budget compliance failures: revenue spend and expenditure below the de minimis threshold incorrectly coded to capital, contrary to funding conditions. More significantly, "repairs and maintenance budgets had not been used effectively to address significant estate priorities in individual schools, resulting in the Council having to complete urgent reactive works funded from central capital allocations."
findings.matters: Schools not deploying their maintenance budgets to planned priorities means central capital is being redirected to emergency reactive maintenance instead of strategic capital investment. This indicates either inadequate school budgets, weak budget discipline, or both—each a concern for estate sustainability and long-term capital planning.
findings.figures: 0 Priority 1 actions, 9 Priority 2 actions identified; revenue miscoding and unexecuted maintenance priorities noted but amounts not quantified
findings.quote: repairs and maintenance budgets had not been used effectively to address significant estate priorities in individual schools, resulting in the Council having to complete urgent reactive works funded from central capital allocations.

findings.paper_title: A&G20260916R7 Internal Audit Progress Report Sept 2026 AG FINAL
findings.headline: Adult social care provider overpayments identified, attributed to guaranteed minimum volume calculation errors.
findings.detail: Before the audit, the Home First System Lead identified that strategic providers had been overpaid on reablement episodes following Discharge to Assess referrals. The overpayments resulted from how guaranteed minimum volumes (GMVs) are processed in the payment system. Overpayments are being recovered with new reconciliation arrangements introduced. This issue was also flagged in the 2023/24 Payments to Providers audit, with the management action only recently fully implemented after a two-year gap.
findings.matters: Documented overpayments to service providers indicate payment control failures. The two-year delay to remediate a prior-year finding raises questions about remediation capacity and financial oversight of commissioned services.
findings.figures: Overpayment amount not quantified in this report; flagged in both 2023/24 and 2026/27 audits
findings.quote: Prior to the audit, the Home First System Lead identified that strategic providers had been overpaid for some reablement episodes which followed D2A care, due to the way in which payments are processed to take GMVs (guaranteed minimum volumes) into account. Overpayments are in the process of being recovered and reconciliation arrangements have been introduced to ensure accurate payments are now being made.

findings.paper_title: A&G20260916R7 Internal Audit Progress Report Sept 2026 AG FINAL
findings.headline: Forty-one audit recommendations are more than 9 months overdue for implementation.
findings.detail: As of 2 September 2026, 41 management actions from previous audit reports remain open and are 9+ months past their original implementation target date. These span multiple service areas: Planning Appeals, Supported Transport, Property Services, ICT, Children's Services, HR, and Adult Services. While some have contextual explanations (IT restructure delaying AI actions), the pattern indicates slow governance capacity across the council.
findings.matters: Slow remediation of audit findings is itself a control weakness. A council that cannot implement identified control improvements promptly suggests systemic governance issues that increase financial and operational risk.
findings.figures: 41 actions overdue 9+ months; separately, as at 10/08/26: 30 actions not implemented and overdue (out of 312 total outstanding actions), 175 actions where partial implementation is reported
findings.quote: As at 02/09/2026 there are 41 management actions open, which are 9 months past their original target date for implementation.

findings.paper_title: A&G20260916R5 TM Q1 Report A&G Final
findings.headline: Council will split into three successor unitary authorities on 1 April 2028 and is actively managing treasury position for the split
findings.detail: Oxfordshire County Council is abolished on 31 March 2028 and replaced with three new unitary councils and a separate Fire & Rescue Service. The Treasury Management Strategy Team is undertaking forecasts to disaggregate the balance sheet and treasury positions across the new entities. As part of this, the council is considering reducing its exposure to pooled funds (currently £92.73m) to ensure sufficient liquid assets are available on vesting day and that each new council starts with a sustainable financial position.
findings.matters: Reorganisation creates medium-term uncertainty around debt allocation, reserves distribution, and the credit profile of each successor council; orderly planning now avoids forced asset sales or illiquidity at vesting
findings.figures: Vesting date: 1 April 2028; pooled funds at 30 June 2026: £92.73m (purchase price £88m); three successor councils plus Fire & Rescue
findings.quote: Work will be undertaken to forecast and disaggregate the balance sheet and treasury positions for the three new successor councils and the Fire & Rescue Service.
